**SPC Studio** does Statistical Process Control in the browser: control charts (is the process stable?), capability Cp/Cpk (does it meet spec?) and Pareto (what to fix first). [Open it](https://garciaralphlawrence-svg.github.io/SPC-Studio/)

Cpk measures how well a process fits inside its spec limits, using within-subgroup variation. Rule of thumb: **Cpk ≥ 1.33** capable, 1.00–1.33 marginal, below 1.00 not capable. Pp/Ppk use overall variation instead.
Signal rules: 1) a point beyond 3σ; 2) 2 of 3 beyond 2σ on one side; 3) 4 of 5 beyond 1σ on one side; 4) **8 points** in a row on one side of the centre; 5) 6 points steadily rising or falling.
Yes — use the **Your Data** tab to upload Excel or CSV. It picks the right chart, reads LSL/USL/Target columns automatically, and the file never leaves your browser. Templates are downloadable.
The Pareto chart ranks problem categories and highlights the vital few that make up about **80%** of the problem — fix those first.
Control charts: **I-MR** (individual values), X̄-R (subgroups of 2–10) and p chart (proportion defective). Plus capability, normality and Pareto.
**Anderson-Darling** test with a normal probability plot. If p < 0.05, treat the PPM estimates with caution.
It shows expected and observed defects per million (PPM), Z.bench and the sigma level (Z.bench + 1.5 shift).
The calculations were checked against SciPy. The demo data (lab turnaround, bottle fill, documentation errors, complaints) is synthetic.

No — all records are **synthetic** (fake but realistic). It's a portfolio demo, not a medical device, and everything runs in the browser.
AUC is about **0.79** for readmission and 0.75 for no-shows, tested on 20% held-out data.
It trains a Logistic Regression and a 30-tree Random Forest in your browser (80% train / 20% test) and uses whichever has the higher AUC.
Daily admissions are forecast with **Holt-Winters** exponential smoothing (trend + weekly pattern) with a 95% range, backtested at about 9% average error.

SPC Studio — Statistical Process Control in the browser, built by Ralph Garcia.
SPC (statistical process control) uses statistics to check whether a process is stable and whether it meets its specification.
It answers three questions: Is it stable? (control charts) Is it capable? (Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk) What do we fix first? (Pareto).
Control charts: I-MR chart for individual values, X-bar R chart for subgroups of 2 to 10, and p chart for the proportion defective with varying sample sizes.
Limits are the centre line plus or minus 3 sigma, using standard constants (d2, A2, D3, D4).

Signal rules (Western Electric rules plus a trend rule): 1) one point beyond 3 sigma; 2) 2 of 3 points beyond 2 sigma on the same side; 3) 4 of 5 points beyond 1 sigma on the same side; 4) 8 points in a row on the same side of the centre line; 5) 6 points in a row steadily increasing or decreasing.
Each signal is explained in plain English, and improvements are marked "better than usual".
Capability: Cp and Cpk use within-subgroup sigma (what the process could do); Pp and Ppk use overall sigma (what it actually delivered); Cpm uses the target.
It also shows expected and observed defects per million (PPM), Z.bench and the sigma level (Z.bench + 1.5 shift).
Rule of thumb: Cpk of 1.33 or more is capable, 1.00 to 1.33 is marginal, below 1.00 is not capable.
One-sided specs (only an upper or lower limit) are supported.
Normality: Anderson-Darling test with a normal probability plot; if p is below 0.05 the PPM estimates should be treated with caution.
Improvement what-if: sliders to move the average or reduce variation and see the new Ppk and defects per million, plus a one-click "centre on target".
Pareto: ranks categories and highlights the vital few that make up about 80% of the problem.
Your Data (upload): upload an Excel or CSV file on the Your Data tab.
It guesses the right analysis and columns, reads LSL, USL and Target columns automatically, supports grouping by a column such as Hour or Batch, and can count raw rows for a Pareto.
Templates can be downloaded.
The file never leaves the browser.
Demo data: lab turnaround time, bottle fill volume, documentation errors and complaint categories — all synthetic.
The calculations were checked against SciPy.
Printing / saving as PDF is built in.

CareSight — Predictive Hospital Analytics, built by Ralph Garcia.

It predicts which discharged patients are likely to be readmitted within 30 days, which outpatient appointments are likely to be no-shows, and forecasts daily hospital admissions for the next 30 days.

Machine learning models: for each prediction it trains a Logistic Regression and a Random Forest (30 decision trees) right in the browser on 80% of the data and tests them on the other 20%; the model with the higher AUC is used.
Accuracy (AUC): about 0.79 for readmission and 0.75 for no-shows.
The decision threshold is tuned for the best F1 score.

Readmission risk factors used: age, length of stay, admissions in the past 12 months, ER visits, number of discharge medications, abnormal labs, heart failure, kidney disease, COPD, diabetes, hypertension, cancer, follow-up visit booked, department, payer and discharge disposition.
The biggest drivers are prior admissions, number of medications, age and length of stay; booking a follow-up visit lowers risk.
No-show prediction uses days booked in advance, SMS reminder, previous no-shows, distance from the hospital, age, clinic, day of week, time slot, payer, new patient and rainy season.
SMS reminders and shorter booking lead times reduce no-shows the most.
Volume forecast: daily admissions are forecast with Holt-Winters exponential smoothing (trend + weekly pattern), with a 95% range, checked by a 30-day backtest (about 9% average error).
It also suggests how many admitting nurses each day needs.

Your Data (upload): upload your own Excel (.xlsx) or CSV file on the Your Data tab and CareSight retrains the models on it — readmission data (needs a Readmitted Within 30 Days Yes/No column), no-show data (needs a No-Show Yes/No column) or daily admissions (Date + Admissions).
Column names don't need to match exactly, blanks are filled automatically, there are downloadable templates, and the file never leaves the browser.
What-If Simulator: change a patient's details (age, conditions, follow-up, medications) and see the predicted risk, the reasons behind it, and suggested actions that would lower it.
Data: all records are synthetic (fake but realistic) — no real patient data.
It is a portfolio demo, not a medical device.
Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded.
